blocks.title: Capablanca writes
blocks.text: "Before you fight for victory in the opening or middlegame, you must master the endgame. One who does not know the endgame cannot be a strong player."
The endgame begins when the most important pieces have left the board and only the kings remain with pawns and perhaps one or two minor pieces.
The king becomes an attacker
This is the **biggest change** in the endgame. The king that fled all game must now actively attack.

items.title: Bring the king to the centre right away
items.text: As soon as you sense the endgame approaching, start moving the king toward the centre of the board. A central king dominates a marginal one.

items.title: Pawns are future queens
items.text: Every pawn that reaches the last rank becomes a queen (or another piece). This is the main goal in pawn endgames.

blocks.text: The rule of pawn promotion
Capablanca explains this rule clearly and precisely:

blocks.title: The key rule
blocks.text: For a pawn endgame to be winning, **the king must be ahead of its pawn** with at least one empty square between them. If the enemy king is directly in front of the pawn — it’s a draw!

items.title: Advance the king, not the pawn
items.text: Capablanca advises: advance the king as far as possible without endangering the pawn. Move the pawn only when it is necessary for its protection.

items.title: The secret weapon — "the Opposition"
items.text: When two kings face each other with an odd number of squares between them, the player who **moved last** has the advantage. It is called the opposition — and it is key to all pawn endgames.

blocks.text: A cardinal principle

blocks.title: One holds two — Capablanca’s principle
blocks.text: "A pawn that holds two enemy pawns is one of the master’s main tools." If your pawn blocks two of the opponent’s, you are effectively a piece ahead — use that advantage on the other side of the board!
Bishop vs. Knight in the endgame

items.title: The bishop is stronger when pawns are on both sides
items.text: Thanks to its range the bishop can attack pawns on both wings at once. The knight is slow and cannot reach everywhere.

items.title: The knight is stronger in closed positions
items.text: When the pawns are locked and the position is closed, the knight is better because it can jump over pawns and reach the ideal square.

blocks.title: The bishop’s weakness — the rook pawn
blocks.text: If your pawn heads to h8 (or a8) and that square is the opposite colour to your bishop, the opponent holds the corner and it’s a draw! Capablanca especially highlights this as the source of many missed wins.
Checkmate and draw

blocks.title: Check
blocks.text: A situation where the king is under attack. The player **must** defend — move the king, capture the attacker, or place a shield in between.

blocks.title: Checkmate — end of the game
blocks.text: The king is under attack and there is no legal way to defend. The game ends here — the king is never actually captured.

blocks.title: Stalemate — the winner’s nightmare!
blocks.text: The player to move is **not in check**, but has no legal move. It’s an immediate draw! This is the most dangerous mistake in the endgame — turning a winning position into a draw with one bad move.

items.title: Repetition of position
items.text: If the same position occurs **three times**, a draw can be claimed.

items.title: Insufficient material
items.text: Only kings, or king + bishop/knight against king — checkmate is impossible. Automatic draw.

blocks.text: About the author

blocks.title: José Raúl Capablanca (1888–1942)
blocks.text: A Cuban chess player, the third official World Chess Champion. Regarded as one of the greatest chess geniuses of all time — known for a crystal-clear playing style and intuitive understanding of position.

Capablanca learned chess at just **four years old** by watching his father. He never attended a chess school — he learned it all himself, by playing. At only 13 he beat the Cuban champion Juan Corzo and became a national sensation.
In the period **1916–1924** he did not lose a single game. He won the world championship title in 1921, defeating the legendary Emanuel Lasker, who had been champion for a full 27 years.

items.title: Photographic precision
items.text: He won through simplicity and perfect technique — not aggression.

items.title: A populariser of chess
items.text: He wrote "Chess Fundamentals" (1921) precisely for beginners and amateurs.
